articles.title: How Bacardí and AMC Resurrected the Crypt Keeper After 30 Years
articles.fullContent:
By Bill Bradley Join ADWEEK CEO Will Lee, senior brand marketers, and industry leaders at our ADWEEK Exchange Series, to discover how measuring real audience attention—not just impressions—drives smarter, higher-ROI CTV strategies. Two more stops in NYC and Boston next week with brand speakers from Havas, Hartz, Wayfair, WHOOP, SharkNinja, and more. Seats are limited.

The Crypt Keeper is back, but to resurrect the Tales From the Crypt icon, AMC had to find a partner with the right… spirit.

That’s right, boys and ghouls. After a 30-year absence, the Crypt Keeper, along with his original voice artist, John Kassir, has returned to host AMC’s 30th anniversary of FearFest, and spirits company Bacardí helped make it happen.

Over the course of FearFest and its 650 hours of horror content in October, AMC and Bacardí will release five vignettes featuring the Crypt Keeper across linear and social. And for those who want even more Crypt Keeper, all seven seasons of Tales From the Crypt are now streaming on AMC+ and Shudder for the first time.

“The idea of bringing [the Crypt Keeper] back for the first time, resurrecting him from the crypt, if you will, just seemed so fun and on brand,” Lisa Pfenning, VP for Bacardí Rum in North America, told ADWEEK. “We share a lot of the same values, the Crypt Keeper and Bacardí.”

Those values include self-expression and good humor—yes, the Crypt Keeper’s signature puns are back. And with the added bonus of Halloween themes and ’90s nostalgia, Pfenning called the stunt a natural partnership.

But bringing the Crypt Keeper back after three decades wasn’t just some easy hocus pocus. According to Bacardí and AMC, the companies spent months bringing the character to life.

Bacardí had previously teamed up with AMC for FearFest in 2025, and coming into this year, the brand wanted to make an even bigger splash to own Halloween. To get things started quickly, conversations kicked off in early 2026, according to Mike DiGiacomo, head of integrated marketing and Content Room, AMC Global Media.

At the time of those initial conversations, AMC didn’t have the streaming rights to Tales From the Crypt, but as the months went on and the licensing deal was finalized, the idea of bringing back the Crypt Keeper for original content began to catch on.

“We were like, ‘This could be something,'” DiGiacomo said, adding, “When we first presented the idea of partnering with the Crypt Keeper to Bacardí, their eyes lit up. All we had to say was ‘Crypt Keeper,’ and we hit the ground running.”

The team got to work on multiple rounds of creative, integrating the Crypt Keeper into Bacardí’s music-inspired campaign, “Better With a Beat”; recruiting horror effects master and Walking Dead director Greg Nicotero to update the Crypt Keeper’s look and direct the Crypt Keeper content, which included Kassir as the voice; and weaving in Bacardí throughout the process.

“Our whole thing is authenticity. We know that there is a very dedicated audience behind this franchise, so if we’re going to do it, if we’re going to bring Crypt Keeper back, we want to do it right,” DiGiacomo said.

Crypt Keeper is known for showing up in different sketch situations, such as taking on the role of a creepy Santa Claus or acting like a barber with towels hot enough to melt someone’s face off. This time, Crypt Keeper is coming back as a cocktail-loving DJ to work within the Bacardí theme, and you may even see some of the signature Bacardí “Spookito” cocktails on display, which are a mojito with a bloody grenadine twist.

AMC also noted that utmost care was taken with his look and in walking the line so the content didn’t feel too commercial.

“If I’m a fan and I’m watching Tales From the Crypt on Shudder, and I get fed this content, am I going to call that out as an ad, or am I going to actually take that as real content?” DiGiacomo said. “Across the board, no matter who the advertiser is, no matter what the platform or the IP is, that’s first and foremost when it comes to partnerships.”

Regarding Crypt Keeper’s slightly updated look and attire, DiGiacomo noted it came down to relying on experts like Nicotero and the creative team being fans themselves.

“One of the secret sauces we have and something that we talk to brands about a lot is that we’re all fans too, which really makes a difference,” DiGiacomo said. “The people on my team who are working on this project are fully leaned in, and are fans of the genre and the series itself.”

Fans can obviously be opinionated around iconic IP, and though there are detractors about the Crypt Keeper’s updated look, there are also plenty of supporters. And AMC and Bacardí noted that there’s been positive feedback both internally and externally.

“Consumer feedback has been great. We’ve been watching the comments. People are excited to bring him back. They’re excited that the show is being rerun,” Pfenning said.

So what happens next? Will the Crypt Keeper return? Could there be more Tales From the Crypt episodes in the future?

“Yet to be seen if the Crypt Keeper makes a comeback next Halloween,” Pfenning said. “But we will continue to nurture our relationship with AMC for sure.”

On specific future plans, Bacardí is as silent as the grave. But it is a spirits brand, so there’s always a… shot.

AMC Comes Into Upfront With Bite, New Ways to Work With Advertisers Bill Bradley

Bill Bradley is Adweek's deputy TV, Media and Sports editor.

articles.title: ADWEEK’s Agents of Change: Leading With Purpose to Reshape Our Industry
articles.fullContent:
By Brandon Hardin Being the change you want to see in the world requires vision, courage, and the willingness to walk your own path.

ADWEEK’s 2026 Agents of Change, presented by Empower, celebrates the leaders reshaping marketing, media, advertising, and tech through meaningful action.

In partnership with Empower, the industry platform created by Propeller Group and WACL, this award recognizes individuals who combine commercial excellence with a commitment to creating a more responsible and forward-thinking industry.

Chief Content Officer, The Female Quotient

The Female Quotient began as a small experiential company, and along the way transformed into one of the largest communities of women in business. That shift happened largely through content, which has been led by Rachel Apirian since 2018. In that time, she’s grown The FQ community from 18,000 members to 8 million by carefully choosing the voices to elevate, tackling topics that seem far from business such as caregiving and making them relevant to corporate leaders, and always bringing listeners into the conversation. This uniquely empathetic, human-centric view of work has grown The FQ into a media company that generates 3 billion organic social impressions and creates branded content for over 200 companies annually, with engagement rates up to seven times higher than platform averages.

Co-founder & Managing Partner, Exverus by Brainlabs

Talia Arnold and her co-founders built Exverus around a radical idea: People shouldn’t have to sacrifice family, health, or ambition to succeed in advertising. Twelve years later, that philosophy has become a competitive advantage for the full-funnel media agency. The leadership team is over 70% women and people of color, while flexible schedules, three months of paid family leave, unlimited PTO, and just one weekly office day for Los Angeles staff help working parents meet all of their obligations—and advance. Twice-yearly retreats bring remote employees together, while bonuses reward ideas that make it into client media plans. Under Arnold’s leadership, Exverus grew into a multimillion-dollar independent agency before joining Brainlabs, where its people-first culture will remain in place.

Chief Strategy Officer for North America, VML

Keeping a personal touch can be difficult when you’re the chief strategy officer of a 600-strong team overseeing $1.2 billion in business. But VML’s Ellie Bamford is beloved for ensuring visibility and advancement for underserved colleagues, while championing new technology such as the proprietary Foresight Engine to let strategists do what they do best. Her work has raised strategy group billability from 68% to 98% through operational transformation, and has driven nearly $200 million in new business revenue in the past two years. Bamford is also a trusted authority in shaping industry standards, serving on festival juries, hosting workshops, and mentoring junior talent.

Victoria Beaty has spent more than 15 years showing the value of marketing while expanding who gets to be seen and given opportunities. At the urban farming advocacy Growing Places Indy, she used integrated storytelling to help secure more than $1 million in grants and donations, while expanding food-access programs and donating thousands of pounds of produce. She later founded Indianapolis’ first Black-owned plant shop, using it to make greenery—and, in turn, wellness—more accessible through free workshops and forging high-profile partnerships with the WNBA and Indiana Pacers. Her most recent venture, House & Kin Creative, is a principal-led agency where culture and community are essential to outcomes.

To Jared Belsky, leadership means a willingness to take risks—comfort, dollars, and even reputation—to make change real. The Acadia CEO instituted direct media buying across accounts and, in February, returned high-six-figure rebates to 53 clients from 2025 media buys. By rejecting principal-based media buying, he gave up nearly $3 million in potential profit, arguing agencies should earn from agreed-upon fees, not by hiding incentives. Belsky has taken the fight industrywide, launching SayNoToPrincipalMediaBuying.com, partnering with the ANA on education for procurement teams, and creating ItsYourRebate.com to help brands ask tougher questions of their agencies. Meanwhile, Acadia has kept on growing, adding 30 clients in 2026 with an 80% pitch-win rate.

Alan Brown has been building the infrastructure for a more equitable advertising industry, particularly for LGBTQ+ talent. At indie agency DNA&Stone, he co-created Project Violet, connecting emerging queer creatives and strategists with industry mentors, and launched Come Out to Work, helping agencies create cultures where LGBTQ+ employees can be themselves. Internally, 92% of DNA&Stone’s new hires in 2025 identified as women, BIPOC, or LGBTQ+; the agency also holds annual salary audits to address the gender pay gap, along with standardized leveling and equity tracking. Brown also championed Black Black Friday, generating $1.5 million in media support and $250,000 in sales for Black-owned businesses, and led “Poison the Fantasy” during the FIFA World Cup to confront sex trafficking around major sporting events.

Chief Creative Officer for the Americas, Dept

The path to career advancement is not always clear for underrepresented talent. As founder of Asians in Advertising, Bernice Chao has grown the organization to more than 9,000 members, creating a leadership program with 75 graduates, 690 mentorship pairings, four industry summits and the AIA Awards. She even reaches talent before they graduate into the industry as a professor at Loyola Marymount University for the past five years. She has taught 250 students, some of whom have gone on to win the Effies Cannes Collegiate Competition for four consecutive years. Chao also co-authored The Visibility Mindset, a No. 1 Amazon bestseller giving Asian American professionals tools to advance in the workplace. Her impact has been recognized by the AAF Hall of Achievement, The Advertising Club of New York’s Icon Award, Adcolor’s Catalyst Award, and She Runs It Mother of the Year.

Bobbie’s brand was built on a simple insight: Being a new parent comes with too much advice and not enough support. Kim Chappell has turned formula maker Bobbie’s marketing into a platform for destigmatizing how babies are fed through the unconventional move of amplifying the underrepresented voices of actual parents. But feeding babies is not the only hurdle Bobbie is committed to supporting caregivers through—Chappell has also been instrumental in pushing policymakers on paid leave and expanding resources for maternal health. Her “B is for Bobbie” campaign with Cardi B drove major gains in awareness, trust, and consideration while generating 4,000 hotline calls and over 1,000 messages to Congress. By making advocacy part of Bobbie’s business strategy, Chappell has driven brand love in a category that’s otherwise barely discussed in mainstream forums.

To measure success, Christopher Crawford prefers to look at the opportunities an agency creates, not just the creative work it puts out. At Elite Media, he has invested more than $2 million directly into Harlem, including Keep It 100, an entrepreneur pitch competition designed to back emerging creators and future agency owners. His Schoolys initiative at Teachers College Community School provided 50-plus staffers with $150,000 in self-care and professional-development grants, contributing to a 100% increase in staff retention and stronger reported well-being. Crawford also invests in startups addressing financial and health inequities and partners with Harlem nonprofits, and hires people with lived experience rather than through traditional pipelines to make it all happen.

The irony of experiential marketing is that it demands extensive experience to get your foot in the door. As the founder of bicoastal hospitality agency Viper, Celeste Durve is changing who gets to build a career in the experiential space, growing the business to seven figures by creating paid, accessible pathways into an industry often gated by degrees and connections. Her 340-person W-2 workforce gets hands-on experience with brands including Google, Amazon, e.l.f. Cosmetics, and HBO, paving the way to frontline roles in management and corporate leadership. Through the Viper Next Gen initiative for college students and her 290,000-reader Smart Is Sexy media platform, Durve extends that mission beyond her company, equipping women and underrepresented talent with skills, mentorship, and access to influential networks.

Creating technology that serves people and engages audiences is at the heart of everything Miguel Espada does. At SpecialGuestX, the mathematician-turned-creative pairs cutting-edge AI with human-centered storytelling, turning complex research into work with the power to change how people act. From turning Google’s WeatherNext2 into a user-friendly tool for industries from farming to logistics, to pioneering real-time generative AI in live sports at the 2026 NBA Draft, Espada ensures technical innovation serves its intended audience, helping drive 5x revenue growth. He’s equally committed to changing who gets to shape that future, hiring across disciplines and co-founding AI Forum, which has opened conversations on women, queer communities, and AI in Latin America, widening who gets to shape AI’s future.

The joyful disruption of brothers Darain Faraz and Sheeraz Gulsher has improved the lot of creatives all over the U.K. Their joint mission of achieving greater equity for ethnic minorities in the creative industry crystallized in 2019 into People Like Us, the award-winning nonprofit combining creative campaigns, advocacy, and community infrastructure to drive measurable change. The organization has supported more than 3,000 professionals through mentorship, career support, and community events, while pushing the broader U.K. industry to confront salary disparities through a five-year pay gap study. In March 2026, their evidence-based lobbying helped push mandatory ethnicity pay gap reporting onto the government agenda, culminating in the U.K.’s formal commitment to the Equality (Race and Disability) Bill. That’s advocacy with staying power.

CEO & Principal, Zambezi Owner & President, Cornett Co-founders, Own It

Opening their own agency is a dream for many creatives, but the path can be difficult to walk for underrepresented talent. Jean Freeman and Christy Hiler have been paving the way since 2022, when the Zambezi and Cornett leaders co-founded Own It to give women and nonbinary entrepreneurs the data, mentorship, and networks needed to build businesses of their own. Since they came on the scene, women-owned agencies have grown from less than 1% of the industry in 2022 to 4% in 2026, with Own It’s database now spanning more than 1,000 agencies. In 2026, they brought Own It to Cannes Lions and With expanding summits and its first global event at Cannes Lions. Hiler is also one of the founding members and leaders of BLAC, which connects Black and underserved talent with agency internships.

Independent Chilean agency Inbrax does so much more than creative work under the guidance of co-founder and CCO Pancho González. He’s built platforms that give Latin American talent, ideas, and perspectives a bigger stage such as Retail Media Summit Latam, which was founded by González and has grown into a 500-plus-person regional gathering that’s expanding into Peru, Colombia, and Mexico. He’s also pushing independent agencies into AI through IXAI, and broadening DEI representation with Inbrax’s Belong Lab. Inbrax has been recognized as Chile’s Agency of the Year by global creative performance index TopFice for four consecutive years (2022–2025), while González himself has accumulated more than 250 international recognitions for his leadership and creative output.

For three decades, Nicki Harkrider-Probey has been changing local media from the inside out. From pioneering local CTV at Premion—bringing streaming ads to local markets years before that was considered a viable category—to now helping Madhive bring data-driven advertising to local businesses, she has consistently moved ahead of the market. But her most lasting impact has been the people she’s mentored: 31 station sales leaders she developed advanced into director or general manager roles between 2016 and 2024, with a deliberate focus on sponsoring and promoting women into leadership. Her approach to managing is equally direct: Listen, understand what people need, and work to make it happen.

For the past 15 years, Jen Harrington has led Hatch as one of 1% of woman-owned independent agencies and has thrived on her own terms. Alongside the creative work, Harrington has worked tirelessly to help other women achieve their goals too. Through her Eat In or Dine Out video series, she’s brought executive concerns out of the boardroom to be aired around a kitchen table, demystifying leadership, while directing a portion of agency proceeds (and staff time) to art education and food insecurity. Hatch’s Cultural Advisory Council, launched in 2023, brought together marketing professionals spanning different ages, ethnicities, sexual orientations, and career backgrounds to counter the stereotypes being surfaced by AI. In the past three years, she’s also expanded Hatch’s business beyond creative by bringing on industry veteran Dorothy Urlich to build (and own) Hatch Talent, a new revenue engine serving brands’ hiring needs. She also built a Cultural Advisory Council spanning identities and generations to challenge AI-driven stereotyping before it reaches the work.

Emma Harris turned a life-threatening cardiac arrest into a challenge to an industry addicted to burnout. Through SlowTheF*ckDown, the Glow London founder has reached more than 200,000 people on four continents through keynotes, workshops, and leadership programs, giving teams permission to slow down and gain the space and clarity to reduce wasted effort and instead work together. Harris pairs that advocacy with commercial rigor, helping brands including BT, Bupa, easyJet and Virgin improve focus, alignment, and performance. As global chair of The Marketing Academy Alumni, she also champions women and underrepresented talent, promoting wellbeing as essential to creating good work. So next time you’re deciding whether to take on yet another project, remind yourself of one of Harris’ mantras: Busy is not a strategy.

To change the advertising world, Sally Henderson works to make its leaders feel supported. For 15 years, her High-Stakes Leadership Mentoring program has combined coaching, counsel, and practical guidance for executives navigating pressure and pivotal decisions. Her REAL Method (Role, Emotion, Acceleration, Leadership) makes the often-overlooked “how” of leadership tangible, while her pro bono work opens doors for people facing redundancy or transitioning to a new phase of their career. For the past three years, Henderson has mentored Marketing Academy scholars and fellows; she also gives free talks to hundreds annually and supports gender-equity organizations including WACL. In 2026, her research-based book, The HOW of High Performance, became an Amazon No. 1 bestseller in three categories.

Head of Innovation, Fenton Communications

For nearly two decades, Shakirah Hill Taylor has challenged the notion that purpose and performance are competing priorities. At “social good” agency Fenton Communications, she’s personally recruited and developed every member of five digital teams, grown revenue, and turned public interest campaigns into measurable change. Taylor grew the Carton Council account into a $2 million portfolio while expanding digital practice revenue by 20%, and rebuilt an underperforming team into an award-winning operation. Her biggest impact, however, is the people she’s developed, with former mentees now leading digital teams themselves. Through ColorVision, Taylor mentors women of color entering the industry, while her advocacy for health equity and Medicaid doula coverage as a 2024 Black Futures Lab Public Policy Fellow confronted racial disparities in health care.

Having spent most of her life in the spotlight, Paris Hilton understands media, marketing, and commerce as well as anyone at an agency. As the head of her own media company, 11:11 Media, she’s used her platform to mobilize her audience in backing issues including child welfare, neurodiversity, and women-owned businesses. Her advocacy helped drive the federal Stop Institutional Child Abuse Act and 16 state laws protecting more than 15 million children. She has also partnered with Understood.org and Google on the digital series Inclusive by Design about creating intentional spaces that support mental health, while her investigative TikTok series “Searching for Mr. Deepfakes” topped 26 million views in its first week. She’s fueled it all through 11:11 Media’s flywheel of content and commerce spanning entertainment ventures, brand partnerships, and consumer products.

The era of women’s sports has arrived, and its fans are looking to specialized media companies to keep up with the action. Ellen Hyslop co-founded The Gist in 2018 as an editorial platform by women and for women, in an industry where women once represented less than 18% of sports journalists and female and non-binary athletes received less than 5% of coverage. Today, 90% of The Gist’s employees and its entire editorial team are women who focus on storytelling and building fandom instead of getting mired in stats. The platform spans newsletters, social media, a podcast (co-hosted by Hyslop), and events, becoming one of the fastest-growing in sports media with more than 40 million fans engaged each month and revenue growing by 100% year-over-year in 2025.

articles.title: ChatGPT Gets GPT-6 And Intelligent UI For Interactive Answers via @sejournal, @MattGSouthern
articles.fullContent:
OpenAI is releasing GPT-6 in ChatGPT worldwide, introducing the new Intelligent UI that combines text, visuals, and interactive features. The update is rolling out beginning today in the Chat tab for Plus, Pro, Business, and Enterprise users, and will extend to Free and Go users from tomorrow.

In Chat, GPT-6 operates on GPT-6 Sol for the plans included in today’s rollout and on GPT-6 Luna for Free and Go. Enterprise access varies based on admin configurations, and the models supporting ChatGPT Work and Codex stay unchanged with this update.

The company’s help page explains that GPT-6 replaces the ‘Latest’ option in the model menu, while GPT-5.6 Sol stays available as a separate option. The Intelligent UI feature is gradually being introduced on the web and supported, updated apps, at thinking levels from Instant to Extra High. The Pro thinking level continues to run on GPT-6 Astra but doesn’t support this feature, and neither do the older ChatGPT desktop apps for macOS and Windows.

Sol and Luna launched on Sept. 22 for ChatGPT Work, Codex, and the API, when the company said they weren’t yet available in Chat.

OpenAI says it trained GPT-6 to decide how each response is laid out based on the question. Responses can include buttons, forms, and charts, and ChatGPT can still answer in plain text when that’s the most useful format.

The announcement describes the tool-building this way:

“You can also ask ChatGPT to create a tool for the task at hand, such as a calculator to explore how savings could grow, a bill splitter for dinner with friends, or a game you can play in the conversation.”

ChatGPT already offered interactive charts, added in June, and interactive modules for more than 70 math and science topics, added in March, according to its release notes .

If you prefer fewer visuals, you can turn off the Layout and visuals setting on the web. Keep in mind, though, that some visual elements might still show up, as mentioned on the help page.

GPT-6 can begin providing answers even while it’s still thinking or working with tools, and then share more insights without waiting for the user to ask again.

For questions that need web search, the company says GPT-6 Instant starts answering 44% sooner on average than GPT-5.6 Instant.

It also says GPT-6 makes better decisions about when to look something up and more reliably finds information that supports its answer. In an internal test of difficult problems, it reports that GPT-6 addressed the key aspect of the user’s question more often than GPT-5.6, without giving a figure.

Two of OpenAI’s tool examples, a savings calculator and bill splitter, use generic inputs and public math. In August, I observed that these tools are the easiest for Google’s generative UI to replicate as it began appearing in AI Overviews. Calculator and converter pages might also be challenged by ChatGPT-created tools, which enable users to request and utilize them directly in the chat, eliminating the need to leave the conversation.

OpenAI aims for ChatGPT to gradually create more of the user interfaces needed for daily tasks.

Today’s GPT-6 announcement doesn’t say how sources will appear when responses are presented as charts, comparisons, or tools. As mentioned on ChatGPT’s search help page , answers that incorporate web search results might include citations, which can be accessed via a Sources button whenever it’s available.

articles.title: AI Is Pushing Advertising Back Into the Physical World
articles.fullContent:
By Mark Stenberg This story was originally published in On Background with Mark Stenberg, a free, weekly newsletter that explores the key themes shaping the media industry. You can sign up for it here .

At Advertising Week, amid conversations about agents, creators, and combating fragmentation, an unusual topic kept coming up: out of home.

The relatively fusty advertising channel has, in recent years, taken on renewed relevance. Out-of-home advertising, an industry catchall for media including billboards, wheatpastes, leaflets, and other in-person formats, has benefited from a surprising confluence of tailwinds.

Its digital counterpart, somewhat unimaginatively called digital out-of-home media (DOOH), is increasingly seen as offering the best of both its digital and analog components: unskippable, yet targeted and programmable.

The numbers reflect this renewed interest. U.S. out-of-home advertising revenue grew 10.7% year over year in the second quarter, reaching a record $3.16 billion, according to the Out of Home Advertising Association of America . Digital-out-of-home grew even faster, rising 18.5% and accounting for nearly 40% of the category’s revenue.

Taken more broadly, the resurgence of out-of-home reflects a potentially more consequential shift in advertising: As the internet becomes less trustworthy, less trafficked, and increasingly mediated by artificial intelligence, physical space is becoming more valuable.

Dedicated readers of On Background will recognize part of this dynamic. For media companies, in-person events have been one of the few consistent bright spots in an otherwise challenged advertising environment. Publishers from Condé Nast to Semafor to ADWEEK itself have invested significantly in their events businesses, which in some cases now make up more than half of their revenue.

There are several explanations for that growth. The rise of remote work has created a more distributed workforce with fewer consistent opportunities for networking and convening. Events solve that problem neatly.

More broadly, in-person media offers something increasingly scarce: a tangible, memorable experience, rather than the ephemeral one of scrolling past a display ad or skipping through an ad read.

Now, a host of new factors are making that distinction even more meaningful.

The rise of artificial intelligence has unleashed an onslaught of low-quality content—often referred to as slop—whose provenance will only become harder to discern as the technology improves. Consumers are already growing more skeptical of what they encounter online. According to a 2024 Adobe report, 87% of U.S. consumers said the rise of generative AI has made it harder to distinguish fact from fiction online.

That erosion of trust was one of the reasons Mariano Jeger, the former executive creative director at Droga5, cited for his departure to Outfront Media when I spoke to him this past  September. As digital and social content become easier to manufacture and harder to authenticate, brands have new reasons to reconsider the relative value of appearing in those environments.

But AI is changing more than just what consumers encounter online. It is also changing whether they need to visit the open web at all.

Answer engines such as ChatGPT, Claude, and Gemini increasingly answer questions without requiring users to visit the websites from which that information originated. For publishers, that threatens to reduce referral traffic, shrinking the audiences—and ultimately the advertising inventory—that the open web can offer.

Agents could accelerate that shift. Products like Muse and Dots promise to accomplish tasks on behalf of consumers, potentially bypassing not just websites themselves but the advertising that subsidizes them.

Last week, for instance, Amazon blocked Muse from crawling its website. Whatever the specific motivations behind the dispute, it highlights an existential problem for advertising-supported destinations: An agent can extract the utility of a website without ever seeing the ads that help pay for it.

Taken together, these forces—the declining trust in online content, the growing ability to bypass websites, and the rise of intermediaries that don’t consume advertising—could make parts of the digital ecosystem less valuable to marketers.

At the same time, out-of-home advertising has become considerably more sophisticated.

New, eye-catching creative can appear on digital screens programmatically, giving marketers some of the targeting and flexibility they have come to expect online while retaining a defining advantage of physical advertising: You cannot scroll past a DOOH display.

And as more companies have embraced the logic of becoming media businesses, the opportunity has expanded further. Ride shares, airlines, grocery stores, retailers, and other businesses with physical footprints and captive audiences can increasingly turn those environments into advertising inventory.

In a sense, the logic of retail media is escaping retail. Any company that controls a physical space where people spend time has the ingredients to become a media owner.

But the same forces making physical space more valuable to advertisers risk making that space less pleasant for everyone else.

In New York, the phenomenon can already feel like a scourge, as public spaces increasingly give way to kiosks and screens featuring a constant stream of advertising. In a recent episode of his podcast , New York Times journalist Ezra Klein bemoaned the situation.

“A column I have wanted to write—and have not written, in part because I’ve been afraid of the reaction to it—is that as a newcomer to New York City (I moved here three years ago) I find the presence of the advertising on the New York City subway and on the buses really sad,” Klein said.

The natural counterargument is that those advertisements help subsidize public transit, keeping it more accessible for riders. But the M.T.A. receives only about 1% of its operating revenue from advertising, according to Klein. He raises an intriguing question: Would transit users swallow a modest price increase in exchange for an ad-free subway system?

The question points to a tension that will only grow more important if the out-of-home boom continues.

In nearly every advertising channel, marketers must balance reach against frequency. Show someone an ad too many times and its effectiveness declines; eventually, familiarity becomes annoyance. Online, advertisers can use frequency caps to limit that exposure. And consumers retain an even simpler option: They can set down their phones, turn off the television, or put away the magazine.

articles.title: How to build brand loyalty: 7 strategies that work for 2026
articles.fullContent:
Key takeaways

  1. Brand loyalty is the emotional connection that drives customers to repeatedly choose one brand over alternatives, even when cheaper or more convenient options exist.
  2. Loyal customers cost less to retain than new ones cost to acquire, spend more over time, and actively recommend the brand to others.
  3. Building brand loyalty in 2026 requires consistent experiences, personalized engagement, fast customer care, and smart use of AI to anticipate customer needs.
  4. Key metrics for tracking brand loyalty include net promoter score, customer lifetime value, engagement rate, and sentiment analysis.

What is brand loyalty?

Brand loyalty is the connection between a brand and a customer that drives someone to make repeat purchases from a specific brand. They stick with that brand even when alternative suppliers or products may be cheaper or more easily accessible.

The lineup outside the Apple Store to get the latest iPhone the first morning it’s available? That’s brand loyalty in action.

What separates loyalty from habit is the emotional connection behind the purchase. A habitual buyer picks your product because it’s there. A loyal customer picks it because it says something about who they are, and because they trust you to deliver. That trust is built over time through familiarity with your brand (also known as brand awareness), satisfying early experiences, and consistency after the sale.

[contentuprade]

Brand loyalty vs. customer loyalty

Brand loyalty and customer loyalty sound interchangeable, but they come from different places. Brand loyalty is emotional and identity-driven. Customer loyalty is usually transactional, powered by price, points, or convenience. Both are worth having, but only one survives a competitor’s discount.

The brand loyalty pyramid

The brand loyalty pyramid was developed in the 1990s by David Aaker, hailed as “the father of modern branding.”

Just as the sales funnel shows how potential buyers move through the conversion process, the brand loyalty pyramid shows how customers move through the process to becoming brand-loyal.

The pyramid has five stages:

  • Switchers: People who have bought your product but are just as likely to buy a competitor’s product next time.
  • Habitual buyers: People who buy your products out of habit but could easily be swayed to another product if it’s cheaper or more convenient.
  • Satisfied buyers with switching costs: People who are satisfied with your brand but primarily stick with your products because there are barriers to switching (such as learning how to use a new tool or platform, or having to buy new cords or accessories).
  • Buyers who like the brand: At this point the connection becomes emotional, and the buyer becomes passionate about your brand for reasons they may not be able to articulate clearly.
  • Committed buyers: These are the people lining up to buy a new product the moment it launches. They love your brand and aren’t afraid to show it.

Source: Aaker, D.A. (1991) Managing Brand Equity. The Free Press, New York.

Why is brand loyalty important?

Brand loyalty matters because it lowers what you spend to grow and raises what each customer is worth. It’s obvious that you want people to choose your brand over your competitors. Brand loyalty ensures they do so again and again. But it provides more value to your brand than the simple revenue from customer retention and each purchase. Here’s why.

How loyal customers reduce acquisition costs and increase lifetime value

Acquiring a new customer is harder (and more expensive) than selling to a repeat customer.

Part of that is targeting efficiency. The more interaction you have with a customer or prospect, the better you can personalize your offers. Plus, you can target specific conversion goals (upsell? refill?) rather than using CPM awareness marketing campaigns.

Loyalty also cushions you when budgets tighten. When consumers cut back, the brands they already trust are the ones they keep buying, which makes retained revenue more predictable than new-customer revenue during uncertain periods.

Brand loyalty increases your lifetime customer value. That, in turn, increases the amount that you can afford to spend on customer acquisition and increases the ROI of your social marketing strategy.

Why loyal customers drive word of mouth and advocacy

Loyal customers do more than buy your products themselves. They share their love for your product with others, which turns retention into a growth channel. That value shows up in written customer feedback and in everyday word of mouth.

Word of mouth is the most common source of brand discovery among internet users in the United States. And shared social content (the digital version of word of mouth) is the most powerful way to turn brand awareness into consideration.

What drives brand loyalty?

Loyalty isn’t one big gesture. It’s the accumulation of small, repeated signals that a brand is reliable and worth caring about. Researchers

articles.title: As Fox News Celebrates 30 Years, Two Originals Share Stories of the Early Days
articles.fullContent:
By Mark Mwachiro Fox News is celebrating an important milestone on Wednesday as it turns 30.

The network is marking the occasion with continued ratings success: During the just-concluded quarter , Fox News remained the most-watched cable network in total viewers and the advertiser-coveted Adults 25-54 demo during primetime and total day.

It has been the No. 1 network in total viewers during primetime for the past three quarters and has remained the most-watched network in total viewers during total day for 22 consecutive quarters.

Two of the network’s executives behind its long-running success, Meade Cooper , executive vice president of primetime programming, and Kim Rosenberg , executive vice president of news programming, are Fox News originals and have been there since its launch in 1996.

In honor of the network’s 30th anniversary, the duo looked back on Fox News’ early days, sharing stories of how far it’s come since then.

30 years of breaking news, covering elections, and reporting on the issues you care about most. Thank you for making us a part of your daily lives since 1996. 🇺🇸 pic.twitter.com/V9ZTCTVeiB

Cooper: I started a month before the network launched. We all gathered at a nearby Hilton for a welcome presentation and then walked down 6th Avenue to headquarters. I learned I would be working as a production assistant on Hannity & Colmes (then known as Hannity & Liberal to be determined). I met a group of smart, hardworking people who were ready to tackle this incredible, unpredictable job.

Rosenberg: It was my first job out of college—here I was, a 21-year-old theatre major, walking into a newsroom under construction, at a network getting ready for launch. It was chaotic and overwhelming in the best possible way. I was excited and a little nervous about how it would all unfold. And whether I could get through the first day without accidentally crossing in front of the studio camera.

Tell us about a pain point that existed in the early days that no longer exists.

Cooper : The news moved at the same pace as it does today, but the tools we had to work with were not quite as quick. Editing video and creating graphics were much more time-consuming. It was more challenging to get guests in the field. We had to send a satellite truck (which was expensive and had limited availability) to get guests and reporters outside of our bureaus and a few other studios. All of this made it more difficult to change things around to react to breaking news.

Rosenberg : When I first became an associate producer, the network was recording all incoming feeds on videotape. We would have to get that video, find an available screener cart, and scroll through until we found what we wanted to run. We would then write down our timecodes on a sticky note and attach them to the boxes to give to the production assistants and editors. It was a very time-consuming process, and it also meant that if another team needed the same video, you had to negotiate for it. If you weren’t a successful negotiator, your show was in trouble. Now, all our incoming video is digital, different producers can screen it simultaneously, and we can edit with the click of a button. It was a complete game-changer for producers.

How has Fox News changed operationally in the past 30 years?

Cooper : We have grown by leaps and bounds from where we were operationally 30 years ago. We could not produce all of our elements from a computer. We used physical videotapes, which we would run from the edit room to playback. To book guests, we flipped through our paper Rolodexes and made calls from our desk phones since we didn’t have cell phones.

Rosenberg : We’ve grown far beyond the original channel. Fox News Media now encompasses platforms including digital, podcasts, Fox Nation, Fox Books, Fox Weather, and Fox Business. So, operationally, we’re no longer producing for a single screen; we’re meeting our audience wherever and whenever they want to find out what’s going on in the world. That said, our fundamental job has not changed one bit: Get people to the story, get the facts of the story right, and get the news to our viewers. The tools and platform are different. But our mission is the same as it was on that first day 30 years ago.

What has been a memorable moment for you from the past 30 years?

Cooper: There are too many memorable moments to pick just one. I was in the control room for the beginning of the bombing of Baghdad in 2003 and for coverage of the Bin Laden raid in 2011. I have been in the newsroom for elections, inaugurations, and conclaves to select a new Pope. I have traveled across the country and around the world.

Rosenberg : One of my most memorable moments is also deeply personal. Earlier this year, I received a devastating medical diagnosis. Months later, I would learn that the initial indication of stage 4 ovarian cancer was incorrect. But I still required major surgery to remove multiple organs. From the first moment, this company supported my family and me in every possible way, from Suzanne Scott and Jay Wallace to the executive assistants and everyone in between. At a time when I was so scared, I felt completely supported. The day of the surgery, my husband and I had decided he would pick up our daughter after school. We wanted to keep things normal for her. So, when I woke up in the ICU, I opened my eyes to see my sister smiling at the side of my bed. On the other side was my best friend, Jon Glenn ; we met at Fox and have worked together for decades. He’d insisted on skipping work that day to sit in the hospital waiting room and make sure I was okay. It’s a cliché that “we’re all family here.” But it’s also true. And it’s part of the reason I love this company. We show up for each other, no matter what.

What is the secret to your longevity at Fox News?

Cooper: I have stayed at Fox for 30 years because I have been able to do a lot of different jobs. Over the years, I have had a handful (well, maybe two handfuls) of job titles, but I have done many other jobs. One of the great things about Fox is that if you work hard and do a good job, you will be given opportunities.

Rosenberg : I know how unusual it is these days for somebody to remain at one company for thirty years. Except here, it’s not that rare. Nearly 100 of us have been working here since launch in 1996. And there are a lot of reasons I think we’ve all stayed. I think one of the biggest is because of the opportunities available: I rose from stage manager to executive vice president. Our CEO, Suzanne Scott, began as a programming assistant. [Fox News president] Jay Wallace was an overnight tape coordinator. I can think of many others with similar trajectories. This company believes fiercely in offering opportunity to those who work hard. And having risen through the corporate hierarchy, we all consider it our duty to help the next generation do the same.

Do you have an interesting story to share from your 30 years of working at Fox News?

Cooper: One year I spent my birthday in Pyongyang, North Korea. A group of North Korean minders sang “Happy Birthday” to me.

Rosenberg : When we first started rehearsing, there were still wires hanging from the ceiling, and workers were putting the finishing touches on everything. Every day was a mad dash to launch. Then, one day, I saw JFK Jr. walking through the newsroom, getting briefed on the business plan, and I thought, “Okay, this job is going to be interesting.”

Mark Mwachiro is a TVNewser contributor who has been writing for the blog since March 2022. Based out of New York, Mark has also contributed to ADWEEK.

articles.title: Email Marketing in the AI Era: Personalization, Automation & Deliverability
articles.fullContent:
Key Takeaways

  • AI adoption in email is concentrated in content production. Personalization, automation, and deliverability, where the bigger revenue gains sit, get far less attention.
  • Personalization is moving from broad segments, like geography and demographics, to individual, predictive targeting.
  • Automation’s share of email revenue grows with company size. Businesses over $51 million in revenue get 71 percent of email revenue from automation versus 11 percent from campaigns.
  • Nearly a fifth of sent emails never reach the inbox, and most of that loss happens before a subscriber has any chance to engage.
  • The programs that win connect personalization, automation, and deliverability into a single system that reinforces itself.

Have you noticed your team is sending more emails than ever, but the results don’t feel any different?

Most marketers are pointing AI at email marketing’s wrong problem. The real opportunity is understanding customer intent, automating decisions, and personalizing experiences at scale. Most teams are using AI to write more emails without fixing the parts of the program that actually drive revenue.

Email personalization, automation, and deliverability are the three areas that actually move that revenue. Inboxes are getting louder as AI makes content creation easier, and louder rarely means more relevant. The rest of this post walks through what’s changing in each area, and how to build them into one connected system.

The AI Shift: What’s Changing in Email Marketing

Marketing teams are under real pressure right now: do more with fewer resources, scale personalization, improve retention and lifetime value, and increase marketing efficiency, all at once. AI looks like the obvious answer.

The problem is where that AI effort is actually going. Ask marketers what their biggest email challenge is today, and list growth tops the list at 29 percent, followed by personalization at 25 percent. Deliverability comes in last, at just 6 percent, even though it’s the foundation everything else depends on. An email that never reaches the inbox can’t be personalized or well-timed enough to matter.

Source

The New Email Marketing Framework

Here’s how the pieces break down:

  1. Personalization: delivering the right message.
  2. Automation: delivering it at the right moment.
  3. Deliverability: making sure it reaches the inbox at all.

You can’t improve these levers in isolation and expect the same lift each time. A gain in one gets erased by a gap in another. Perfect personalization that lands in spam accomplishes nothing, and flawless deliverability paired with generic, one-size-fits-all messaging just means more people ignoring an email they did receive.

Personalization in the AI Era

Most brands are stuck in what amounts to a segmentation trap. They personalize using broad buckets, new versus returning customers, geography, industry, demographics, and call it personalization. Only 34 percent of companies actually use AI-driven or predictive email marketing personalization. Another 24 percent are still at basic audience segmentation, and 5 percent use no personalization at all.

Most teams have the customer data needed for real personalization, they just aren’t using it to predict what happens next. Teams rate themselves strongest in measurement and attribution, with 55 percent calling that capability strong or very advanced. They rate themselves weakest in customer data and identity, at just 37 percent strong or advanced, along with AI skills and governance.

Personalization moves through three stages. Demographic personalization (location, age, gender) is the easiest to set up but produces broad assumptions and low relevance. Behavioral personalization (products viewed, purchases, engagement) produces higher engagement and better conversion. Predictive personalization goes a step further, using purchase likelihood, churn risk, and lifetime value to guide what happens next.

Open rates already vary by age group, from roughly 20.6 percent among 18-24-year-olds up to 25.7 percent among 55-64-year-olds, which makes a strong case for layering behavioral and predictive signals on top of basic demographic segmentation.

articles.title: How JPMorganChase Tapped Togethxr to Reach Women’s Sports Fans Without League Rights
articles.fullContent:
By Trishla Ostwal When media and commerce company Togethxr opened its Togethxr House at the Women’s Final Four in Phoenix this spring, JPMorganChase was one of the brands under its roof.

The brand ran a pop-up shop with Golden State Valkyries guard Tiffany Hayes and Round21, an organization that works with artists in women’s sports. Chase cardholders got access to the product on site.

Being there was partly driven by practicality. “We do not have league sponsorship, so we can’t activate traditionally within the boundaries,” said Tara Bakhle, executive director of sports and entertainment marketing strategy at JPMorganChase, on a panel at the ADWEEK House: Advertising HQ 2026.

Togethxr, founded by women’s sports stars Alex Morgan, Sue Bird, Chloe Kim, and Simone Manuel, sets up near major events without being a sanctioned partner. That gives brands without rights a way to reach fans who travel to those events.

Join Gronk, Coach, The Home Depot, and More at ADWEEK House The audience also makes sense for Chase. The bank compared WNBA and NBA card transactions and found the overlap was between just 5% and 6%. Bakhle said those fans skew younger and more affluent, the customers Chase wants to acquire and keep.

The activation is a reflection of how brands without league deals are finding their way into women’s sports. Deloitte predicts the women’s elite global sports market will reach at least $3 billion in 2026 , up 340% since 2022.

As investment in the space accelerates, media companies like Togethxr are setting up shop around marquee events and selling brands access to fans, athletes, and merch outside sanctioned parts groups. For Chase, the play is about acquiring a larger audience type that its existing sports deals largely don’t reach.

The two companies teamed up again at the WNBA All-Star Weekend in Chicago, where Togethxr recorded its Everyone Watches Women’s Sports podcast live at the Chicago Theatre. Chase offered cardholders presale tickets and hosted a VIP experience for J.P Morgan Wealth Management clients.

Dear Media and Amanda Hirsch Want Brands To Ditch the Script The podcast shares its name with Togethxr’s best-selling product. The company has sold over 200,000 Everyone Watches Women’s Sports shirts, helped by a Nike partnership that took sales global, and has extended the slogan to Stanley tumblers and hats.

Still, fans are getting harder to impress.

“We’re in a current economy in sports where tickets are extremely expensive,” said Bailey Williamson, SVP of partnerships at Togethxr. Fans paying those prices want more out of the day than what happens on the court, she added.

Bakhle said the infrastructure hasn’t kept pace. Rights are split across ESPN, NBC, and others, and “even accessing the programming or finding the game on TV is still actually pretty hard,” she said. Investment also “still does tend to go into the men’s side,” even as new leagues and teams launch.

articles.fullContent:
WordPress has officially released a canonical MCP Adapter plugin that also maintains backward compatibility. Now users who want to add AI functionality to their site can choose the official WordPress MCP Adapter plugin.

MCP (Model Context Protocol) is an open standard developed by Anthropic that lets AI systems securely connect to apps, data, plugins, tools, and websites, enabling AI to access information and perform actions. For WordPress websites, MCP enables AI to interact with sites, plugins, and WordPress functions (PHP code snippets that perform specific tasks like publishing posts).

Jason Adams, Director of Engineering, AI at Automattic tweeted :

“The WordPress MCP Adapter is now released: https://wordpress.org/plugins/mcp-adapter 🎉

This is the canonical MCP plugin for WordPress, carefully architected for backwards-compatibility with MCP versions. If you want MCP in your site or plugins, I highly recommend using this.

…It makes use of the Abilities API to avoid functional redundancy while handling authorization. I’m excited to see the pieces coming together!”

“The backwards compatibility matters. WordPress plugins tend to stay around for years.”

“Agreed, and we can’t control the backwards-compatibility of the MCP protocol itself, so making a way for this in our ecosystem is important.”

The MCP Adapter plugin has been around for some time but it was previously only available through the official WordPress MCP Adapter GitHub releases page , which is why it already has over 40,000 installations. Version 0.70 is the first version to be published in the official WordPress.org repository.

Review the details and download the official WordPress MCP Adapter plugin here or install it through your WordPress admin dashboard.

articles.title: Google’s Search Antitrust Ruling: What Advertisers Should Check Next
articles.fullContent:
This post was sponsored by Silver Arbitration Law, PLLC. The opinions expressed in this article are the sponsor’s own.

If you manage Google Search campaigns, you have explained rising CPCs many times: more competitors, broader match types, a lower Quality Score, an account that needed restructuring. Each explanation is plausible.

I have worked in arbitration since before Google existed, as both counsel and arbitrator. Below I set out what the record shows: what the court found, which auction changes it named and when they ran, and what you would have to establish about your own account before any of it applies to you.

Why The Search Antitrust Ruling Matters For Digital Paid Marketers & Advertisers

In August 2024, after a ten-week trial, the court found that Google “has exercised its monopoly power by charging supracompetitive prices for general search text ads” ( Mem. Op. at 4 ).

Supracompetitive means above the price a competitive market would produce.

The trial record showed that Google’s ads team used internal “ pricing knobs ” that raised what a winning ad paid without any change in bids, ad quality or competition, mostly by inflating the runner-up’s score that sets the winner’s CPC.

Dates Of The Auction Changes That Raised CPCs

Four of these instances have date ranges you can check against your own account:

Format pricing, 2012–2019. Ads using sitelinks, callouts or structured snippets paid more to maintain their position. By 2019 the charges generated about 15% of text ad revenue (UPX0042, UPX0045, UPX0512; Mem. Op. at 84, 86 ; Pls.’ Proposed Findings at 231 ).

Squashing, 2014 onward. Trial exhibits show Google raised the predicted click-through rate of every ad except the leader, which raised the winner’s price without any improvement in the competing ad (UPX0442, UPX0051; Mem. Op. at 83–84 ).

rGSP, 2019 onward. Under rGSP, Google multiplies the runner-up’s score by an adjustable factor; the winner pays against that inflated score or is randomly swapped out of the slot. Projected effect: a 5–6% CPC increase on top slots. No opt-out (UPX1045, UPX0457, UPX0059; Mem. Op. at 85 ; Pls.’ Proposed Findings at 235–236 ).

Advertisers were not told. Google’s Vice President of Ads testified: “We tend not to tell advertisers about pricing changes” ( Tr. 1226, Dischler ). The court found that “[m]any advertisers do not even realize that Google is responsible for the changes in price” ( Mem. Op. at 91–93, 260 ).

Individual advertisers still need to establish whether they were affected and by how much. The first step is to get informed, and there are two ways to do it. You can ask an arbitration lawyer to assess your account; I do this for advertisers, and you can book a short call with me . Or you can read up on the case first: this research prompt has an AI assistant brief you on what the courts found and whether it fits a business like yours.

Start With The Google Ads Spend You Need To Review

The search ruling covers general search text ads. The court did not find a monopoly in the broader market for all search advertising, which includes ads sold by retailers such as Amazon and Walmart. If much of your spend went to Shopping or Performance Max, separate the text-ad portion before drawing conclusions about your account. This research prompt has an AI assistant tell you which ad types and years of spend count.

Clarify The Business & Agency Behind The Account

Note which legal entity accepted Google’s advertising terms and paid the invoices, and which agencies or manager accounts ran the campaigns and when. Those details determine who can review the account and who would raise any claim, and they are the first thing counsel will ask for.

Verify The Court Sources Behind The Search-Ruling Claims

Display spend falls under a second ruling. On April 17, 2025, Judge Leonie Brinkema of the U.S. District Court for the Eastern District of Virginia found that Google had monopolized two parts of the display advertising chain.

That case focused largely on publishers, and the court did not accept every market claim the government brought. If you bought display inventory through Google’s ad tech tools, it raises a separate question about how those transactions worked. Which ruling matters to you depends on the products you used and the years you used them.

Distinguish Findings, Appeals & Unverified Claims

Court findings in this article are quoted with a page cite to the opinion. Anything cited to an exhibit number (UPX, DX) or a transcript (Tr., Dep.) is a trial exhibit or sworn testimony, most of it Google’s own. The two are not the same: a finding is what the court concluded; an exhibit is evidence the court heard.

Google disagrees with the ruling and is appealing . The court’s September 2025 remedies decision requires Google to disclose material changes to its ad auction publicly . Advertisers should therefore have more information about changes that affect what they pay.

Prepare Account-Specific Questions For Counsel

Confirm Applicable Terms, Claim Ownership & Timing

Google’s advertising terms contain an arbitration clause . Advertisers bound by that clause must pursue covered disputes through individual arbitration and waive the right to bring a class action. Each advertiser pursuing such a claim brings it through the American Arbitration Association. The court’s findings provide a starting point; reviewing an account and deciding whether to file remain separate steps.

A claim could be potentially worth 15% to 30% of your eligible search spend. Economists estimate Google’s overcharge at about 5% to 10%, and antitrust law triples proven damages.

If your business spent $10 million on eligible search ads during the relevant period, that points to a potential claim of $1.5 million to $3 million, before fees and case-specific adjustments. That is the size of the claim. An arbitrator or a settlement decides what is paid.

Advertisers ask me this more than anything else. Thousands of U.S. advertisers are already pursuing individual claims, and I am not aware of any reported retaliation against one for filing. Retaliating against a group of claimants that size would create a new legal and reputational problem for Google while two federal courts are overseeing its conduct.

articles.title: How to calculate engagement rate in 2026
articles.fullContent:
Key takeaways

  1. Engagement rate measures how many people interact with your social content relative to reach, impressions, or follower count. It includes actions like likes, comments, shares, and saves, but not passive views.
  2. The most common formula is engagement rate by reach (ERR): total engagements divided by reach, multiplied by 100. Different formulas suit different goals, from organic posts to paid campaigns.
  3. A good engagement rate typically falls between 1% and 5%, but benchmarks vary significantly by platform and industry. Always compare against your specific platform and industry, not a universal standard.
  4. Tracking engagement rate over time shows which content resonates, which formats to prioritize, and where to adjust your strategy. Perch by Hootsuite automates that tracking across all your accounts, and social media analytics tools can also provide industry benchmarks for comparison.

What is engagement rate?

Engagement rate is a social media metric that measures how much of your audience actively engages with your content. It defines the amount of interaction a piece of content (or a campaign, or a whole account) gets compared to reach or audience size.

Engagement metrics vary by channel, but in general, it’s any action someone takes to interact with your content, including likes, comments, shares, saves, poll responses, messages, or link clicks. Because each platform counts engagement a little differently, it helps to know exactly what actions feed into your social media engagement rate before you calculate it.

Why does engagement rate matter?

Engagement rate matters because it shows whether your content is actually connecting with your audience. When people take the time to like, comment, share, or save a post, it’s a strong signal that they find it interesting or useful.

Second, higher engagement rates help you get better visibility on social media platforms. That’s because social algorithms surface more engaging content to new audiences.

A lot of engagement on your content also makes you look more trustworthy and appealing to first-time profile visitors, especially if there’s an active conversation happening in your comments. For enterprise teams, engagement rate is also one of the clearest ways to prove social ROI to leadership, since it ties content performance to real audience behavior.

What counts as engagement on each platform?

Engagement is any action a user takes to interact with your content, but the specific actions that count vary from platform to platform. Knowing what feeds into the formula helps you calculate an accurate engagement rate and compare performance fairly across channels.

Here’s what typically counts as engagement on each major social network:

  • Instagram: Likes, comments, shares, saves, and replies to Stories.
  • TikTok: Likes, comments, shares, saves, and follows generated by a video.
  • Facebook: Reactions, comments, shares, and clicks on links or buttons.
  • LinkedIn: Reactions, comments, shares (reposts), and clicks.
  • X (Twitter): Likes, replies, reposts, quote posts, and clicks.
  • Pinterest: Saves (repins), comments, clicks, and close-ups.

Passive metrics like impressions and views usually don’t count as engagement on their own, since they measure exposure rather than interaction. When in doubt, check the platform’s analytics to confirm which actions it includes before running your numbers.

How to calculate engagement rate (6 formulas)

The standard engagement rate formula is total engagements divided by reach, multiplied by 100. That said, there are six variations worth knowing, because each one uses a different denominator and answers a slightly different question.

  1. Engagement rate by reach (ERR): Most common.
  2. Engagement rate by post (ER post): Best for specific posts.
  3. Engagement rate by impressions (ER impressions): Best for paid content.
  4. Daily engagement rate (Daily ER): Best for long-term analysis.
  5. Engagement rate by views (ER views): Best for video.
  6. Cost per engagement (CPE): Best for influencer marketing or conversion-based campaigns.

1. Engagement rate by reach (ERR): Most common

This is the most common engagement rate formula. ERR measures the percentage of people who interact with your content after seeing it.

Here’s how to calculate engagement rate for a single post:

ERR = total number of engagements on a post / reach of that post * 100

To calculate the average ERR across multiple posts, add together the ERR for each post and divide by the total number of posts:

Average ERR = Total ERR / Number of posts

For example: Post 1 (3.4%) + Post 2 (3.5%) / 2 = 3.45%

Pros: Because not all followers see every post, ERR is often more accurate than follower-based metrics, especially in algorithm-driven feeds. Reach includes both followers and non-followers who discover content through search, shares, hashtags, and recommendations.

Cons: Reach can fluctuate for a variety of reasons, making it a difficult variable to control. ...

articles.title: Holiday shopping is happening earlier than ever, here’s what brands need to know
articles.fullContent:
Halloween candy is still on the shelves, but holiday shoppers are making wish lists and hunting for deals months before the holidays arrive.

But as the shopping season gets longer, budgets are getting tighter. For brands, that means more chances to get in front of consumers, but also more competition for every dollar shoppers spend.

Data from Sprout Social’s Q3 2026 Pulse Survey points to three factors that will define the holiday season: campaign timing, price sensitivity and meeting shoppers where they’re increasingly discovering gifts—on social.

Consumers don’t want earlier holiday campaigns, except when they do

Consumers have mixed feelings about how early holiday marketing should start.

According to Sprout’s Q3 2026 pulse survey, nearly half (49%) say campaigns launched as early as August make them more likely to buy, including 19% who say they’re much more likely. Just 11% say an early start makes them less likely to purchase.

But ask consumers when brands should launch their holiday campaigns and the story changes. Half point to October or November as the ideal window, compared to 21% who prefer August or September. Another 12% say brands should wait until December.

Those findings may seem contradictory, but they point to a distinction between when consumers want holiday marketing to dominate their feeds and when they’re open to discovering seasonal products. Shoppers can be receptive to gift ideas, new products and seasonal inspiration well before they want brands to go all-in on holiday messaging. In other words, an earlier presence can influence what they eventually buy without making it feel like the holiday season starts in late summer.

The sweet spot: Show up early without going all-in. Use August and September to build awareness and consideration, then ramp up your holiday campaign in October and November.

For example:

  • Tease what’s coming: Preview holiday collections, seasonal launches or upcoming offers.
  • Get gift-worthy products on shoppers’ radar: Introduce products consumers might want to add to their lists before they’re ready to buy.
  • Start publishing seasonal content: Share gift inspiration and other useful holiday content that gives shoppers a reason to engage early.

Starting earlier gives you more room to test what resonates before peak shopping begins. Then you can put more support behind the products, messages and offers gaining traction.

Brands are already putting this approach into practice. Fenty Beauty, for example, launched its limited-edition holiday collection in September, giving shoppers an early look at its seasonal products. As of writing, the TikTok has received over 100K views and over 5K likes.

Timing also depends on who you’re trying to reach. Younger consumers are especially receptive to an early start: 66% of Gen Z consumers say campaigns launching as early as August make them more likely to buy, compared to 49% of consumers overall.

Tariffs and price pressure are reshaping purchase patterns

Many consumers see shopping earlier as a way to get ahead of rising prices. More than a third (36%) say they’re starting their holiday shopping earlier specifically to avoid tariff-related price increases. Another 27% aren’t shopping earlier yet but are concerned about prices.

In total, 63% of holiday shoppers are thinking about the impact of higher prices.

Those concerns are also affecting how much consumers plan to spend. More than half (56%) expect to reduce their holiday spending this year because of economic conditions like tariffs and the cost of living. Only 30% say they don’t plan to cut back.

Price sensitivity doesn’t mean every brand needs to compete on having the lowest price. Shoppers may be looking more closely at what they get for their money, so holiday content should make value clear. Highlight product quality, versatility or other details that make a purchase feel worthwhile.

Discounts can also tip the scales: Promo codes shared by brands or influencers are the top purchase driver, cited by 30% of consumers. Lastly, brands with products at multiple price points can also organize gift recommendations by budget, making it easier for shoppers to find options that work for them.

For example, last holiday season, REI shared a roundup of expert picks under $50 on Instagram, with a CTA to check out their larger holiday gift guide.

Consumers are discovering gifts on social this year

Social media now rivals in-store shopping for holiday gift discovery. This year, 46% of consumers say they’ll turn to social for gift ideas and product discovery—the same percentage who plan to browse physical stores.

Where consumers turn for holiday gift ideas:

  • Social media: 46%
  • Physical stores: 46%
  • Recommendations from friends and family: 34%
  • TV: 31%
  • Review sites: 23%
  • AI chatbots: 15%

And social’s influence is still growing. Compared to the 2025 holiday season, 28% of consumers plan to use social more to find gifts this year, while another 50% expect their usage to stay about the same.

That creates an opportunity to reach shoppers before they know exactly what they want to buy.

Think about how easily someone encountering your brand for the first time can understand what you sell, who your products are for and why they’re worth considering. Content organized around recipients, interests, occasions or price points can make that discovery process easier and give shoppers a reason to explore your products further.

Bookshop.org, for example, used Instagram to promote its 2025 holiday gift guide, which curated hundreds of recommendations for different types of readers and paired them with a limited-time discount.

What drives a purchase on social?

Discovery is only the first step. Once shoppers find a product on social, the content surrounding it can influence whether they buy.

According to the Q3 2026 pulse survey, promo codes shared by brands or influencers are the top social-specific purchase trigger at 30%, followed closely by brand posts showing products in action at 28%. One major publication can create awareness, but its effect can fade. A sustained presence across relevant publications creates a different type of signal.

Repeated coverage can reinforce the same core facts about a business across multiple sources. Over time, this can contribute to stronger brand recognition and a clearer understanding of the company’s expertise.

For AI visibility, that consistency matters because AI systems are constantly processing information from across the web.

The temptation in PR has often been to measure success by the biggest placement a campaign can generate. A marquee publication can certainly be valuable, but it shouldn’t be the only objective.

A single article can introduce a company to a new audience. An ongoing stream of relevant coverage can keep reinforcing the brand.

articles.title: What’s Making AI Impact Difficult to Measure for Marketers?
articles.fullContent:
Key Takeaways

  • Brands recommended by ChatGPT were 2.5x more likely to receive a website visit within seven days, according to Similarweb research.
  • Most AI-influenced visits did not arrive through an identifiable AI referral.
  • More than half of AI-influenced visits arrived through search, meaning the AI influence can look like ordinary organic traffic in analytics.
  • Last-click attribution can therefore underestimate the role AI plays in brand discovery and consideration.
  • Marketers need broader measurement frameworks that account for AI’s influence across the customer journey.

AI search is becoming an increasingly important way for consumers to discover brands. But measuring its impact is proving much harder than measuring a traditional referral.

A user might ask ChatGPT for a product recommendation, see a brand mentioned, and then search for that brand on Google several days later. Analytics will record the eventual visit, but it may have no way of knowing that an AI recommendation helped start the journey.

New research from Similarweb highlights the scale of this measurement gap. Brands recommended by ChatGPT were 2.5x more likely to receive a website visit within the following seven days, even when there was no direct referral from the AI platform.

The finding suggests that AI visibility can influence traffic without appearing as AI traffic in a standard analytics report.

For marketers, that’s an important distinction. If AI is influencing customers before they reach a website, measuring only the final click can make the channel look less valuable than it actually is.

What Similarweb Found About AI’s Downstream Impact

Similarweb’s research tracked real user journeys to understand what happens after a brand is recommended in ChatGPT.

Source

AI Recommendations Can Lead to More Website Visits</h3>

Similarweb followed users who asked ChatGPT an industry-related question and received a specific brand recommendation. It then tracked their behavior over the following seven days.

Across finance, travel, and beauty, users who received an AI recommendation for a brand were 2.5x more likely to visit that brand’s website than users who received a recommendation for a competing brand.

The research focused on users who had not previously visited the recommended brand and had not already mentioned that brand in their prompt. This helped Similarweb measure the downstream effect of a recommendation rather than simply tracking people who already knew about a company.

The result provides a useful signal for marketers investing in AI visibility. Being mentioned in an AI answer can influence what consumers do afterward, even when the AI platform doesn’t send the eventual website visit.

Most of the Traffic Doesn’t Look Like AI Traffic

This is where traditional measurement becomes complicated.

Similarweb found that 55.9% of AI-influenced visits arrived through search, compared with 40.4% of visits without AI influence.

In practice, that means a user could see a brand recommendation in ChatGPT, remember the name, and later search for it on Google.

That visit would likely be attributed to organic search.

The AI interaction that helped create the interest would receive no credit.

This is the core AI attribution problem. The measurable traffic is real, but the original source of influence can disappear somewhere between discovery and conversion.

Source

Why Last-Click Attribution Misses AI’s Influence

Last-click attribution works reasonably well when a customer journey is relatively direct. But discovery through AI can introduce additional steps that aren’t captured by traditional referral reporting.

The AI Interaction Happens Before the Measurable Visit

Consider a simple journey.

A consumer asks an AI platform which software tools are best for their business. The platform recommends a brand. The consumer doesn’t click a link. Instead, they continue researching, then return to Google two days later and search for the brand by name.

From an analytics perspective, the final visit may look like a branded organic search.

From the customer’s perspective, however, the journey started with AI.

Engagement is up. Your brand is seeing a spike in mentions. Sentiment is trending positive. People are sharing a hack about one of your new products. They’re all positive signs, but if you can’t translate what they mean to the business, those numbers stay trapped and nothing changes off the back of that good momentum.

That’s where social teams find themselves stuck.
